text: Prioritize a unified test-cube assessment integrating surface observations with internal measurements and their diagnostic correlations (s5:t3–t5; s7:t3–t5). Connect defects clearly to printer settings (s1:t7; s4:t3–t5). Earlier surface-only limits applied to narrower diagnostic requests (s1:t3–t5); later requests explicitly favor internal consistency and structural analysis. Clear numbered checklists were preferred for inspections (s2:t3–t5), but that format is not established for training documents. Practical examples may help (s6:t5), although production-risk and temperature-first preferences were task-specific. These are user statements; no assistant suggestions are supplied. Current equipment, thresholds, and medical-production scope remain unspecified.

For test-cube analysis, prioritize systematic diagnosis of visible surface defects and clear, actionable links to printer settings; exclude unrelated material/infill discussion and preventive adhesion advice (s1:t1, s1:t3, s1:t5, s1:t7; s5:t3, s5:t5). These are explicit user preferences. Tables helped comparisons (s5:t1, s5:t3). A continuous numbered checklist was preferred for morning inspections, not necessarily this training document (s2:t3, s2:t5). Mathematical detail was requested for calibration measurements (s3:t3, s7:t7), while temperature-first organization concerned an SOP (s8:t3); neither is established as a universal requirement.

Prioritize systematic diagnosis of visible test-cube surface defects, explicitly connecting observations to printer settings; avoid drifting into prevention or unrelated material/infill factors (s1:t3–t7; s6:t3–t5). These are direct user preferences, not assistant suggestions. Verified, preferably multiple sources per technical detail would suit training documentation (s2:t3–t7). A numbered checklist may help, but the continuous-checklist preference concerned inspections (s3:t3–t5); later SOP sectioning was welcomed (s8:t3–t7), so it is not universal. Production risk examples and temperature-first organization were requested in other contexts and are not established requirements here (s7:t3–t7; s8:t3).

The user prefers logically organized slides with clear, concise bullet points and simple, focused content (s2:t3, s2:t7; s3:t3, s3:t5). For Google Slides, they explicitly favor no animations and seek avoidance of complex transitions (s2:t3, s2:t5). They endorse simple transitions and reflection pauses in Prezi; these may transfer, but are not explicit current Slides requirements (s4:t3–t7; s5:t3–t5). Printable/PDF accessibility was endorsed for Canvas modules, not mandated for presentations (s1:t3, s1:t5). Prior 30/45-minute durations and specific topic coverage were session-specific (s2:t1; s3:t1).

Prefers clear, logically organized slides with concise bullet points and focused, digestible content (s2:t7; s3:t3,t5). Earlier requested no animations and avoidance of complex transitions (s2:t3,t5). Later explicitly requested and endorsed polls, quizzes, trusted videos, timelines, links, and participation (s4:t1,t3; s5:t1,t3), so simplicity should not exclude interactivity. These are user requests or endorsements, not merely assistant suggestions. Offline PDFs/printability were valued for Canvas modules; applicability to slides is uncertain (s1:t3,t5). Prior lesson durations and topic-specific activities do not establish requirements for this annual review.

The user prefers logically organized, content-focused civics slides with concise bullet points, no animations, and avoidance of complex transitions (s2:t3, s2:t5, s2:t7; s3:t3, s3:t5). Daily-life examples were requested for the Bill of Rights and may help here (s3:t1). Neutral, balanced treatment is valued in discussions (s4:t5). Printable/PDF access was appreciated for Canvas modules, so it is optional here, not an established slide requirement (s1:t3, s1:t5). Earlier 30-/45-minute durations were topic-specific; no current duration is established (s2:t1; s3:t1). These are user-stated preferences; no later reversal appears.
